projects.title: Toggle
projects.description: Full stack whitelabel insurance product for Farmers Insurance subsidiary to sell auto, renters, and homeowners insurance nationwide.
projects.content:
# [gettoggle.com](http://gettoggle.com/)


Toggle Inc. hoped to deliver a seamless insurance experience for users looking to buy (and manage) renters, auto, and homeowners insurance.


Every time you’ve had to call an agent to buy insurance or (especially) make an insurance change, that’s a time you could’ve used Toggle.


![Sample Toggle Renters Flow](/images/content/toggle/toggle-0.gif)


_Disclaimer: we built the end-user application for Toggle but were not responsible for managing customers, handling policies, etc._ 


_Disclaimer 2: None of the screenshots are internal photos, these are real marketing slides and app screenshots from customers / reviewers all found online._


A big challenge for Toggle included **building a scalable solution for all 50 states;** this was <u>compounded by insurance regulations and laws</u> in every state which effectively meant we were building a different variation of the application for every state.


![Auto insurance expansion graphic](/images/content/toggle/toggle-1.jpg)


**I worked** _**heavily**_ **on the auto team**, but throughout around 4 years of working I contributed a lot of work to the <u>homeowners</u>, <u>renters</u>, <u>shared internal developer packages</u>, and <u>a re-themeable Toggle Component library</u>.


# Auto Insurance


The auto product focused on delivering a full user experience and customer focused self-service experience for Toggle Inc. I joined when we started building into other states and helped this effort.


![auto-primary-driver.webp](/images/content/toggle/toggle-2.webp)


Work included tweaking signup flows, allowing users to tweak coverages, and adding features on a state by state basis.


![Optional coverages example in auto](/images/content/toggle/toggle-3.webp)


## Test Everything


One really positive company culture from Sure was the **strong focus on testing across all fronts**. This included unit testing, integration testing, manual QA testing, automated QA testing pipelines, and even a manual UAT.


We strongly prided ourselves on releasing features after thorough testing, and it’s something that has really stuck with me as a core tenet of my engineering philosophy.


## PAIN POINT


The biggest pain point I noticed was we had used a ton of `IF/ELSE` and `CASE` logic to handle different scenarios. This made readability and cognitive understanding really difficult.


## Introducing Configurations


Due to the hard-coded nature of the application, I proposed a system that leveraged configs (JSON) to handle any differences between states including copy, coverage differences, UI elements, etc.


### Hooking into Configs


For frontend UI components, we eliminated a lot of prop-pass through via configs and React Context. This proved a super solid initial solution.


```javascript
// basic example
import useComponentConfig from 'some-config';

const SomeComponent() {
  const { configData } = useComponentConfig('STATE');
}
```


_In order to intelligently choose a state, we had to preserve the state the user had chosen for insurance on the initial signup form._


This approach increased DRY-ness in repositories, allowed better unit testing of components, and also provided the ability to make configurations type safe.


The problem now became one of a proliferation of configuration files. The Toggle app needed to be flexible and configurable per state, and per whitelabel. So if we had 2 white-labels and 50 states, we’d have over 100 configuration files. Truth be told, we never really hit an issue because states generally remained unchanged after release aside from minor copy changes and UI updates.


# Homeowners and Component Libraries


![Example Homeowners Component](/images/content/toggle/toggle-4.png)


For a much shorter time period, I worked on the Homeowners product for Toggle. The work included the same smattering of challenges including releasing to multiple states, accounting for (very) different coverages from auto, handling white-labeling, and using a component library created by great minds like Quinn Elwood.


## Component Library


Quinn spent a lot of time consolidating reusable styles, components, and “smarter” components across the three products we had. Eventually she was able to build a cohesive component library from these.


When Quinn left the company, I and a few others became responsible for maintaining the repository in conjunction with new features across each white-label and product.

projects.title: JPL
projects.description: Contract full stack engineering role focused on implementing support apps for labs scientists to improve their day to day work.
projects.content:
# Working at JPL


The division I worked in, OCIO at the time, focused on delivering internal tooling and custom software applications to the rest of the lab and scientists. My team specifically had a specialized stack in Django + React + Postgres applications that solved needs for MARS2020 and other groups.


## IADS Dashboard - System Consolidation


This dashboard focused on consolidating application data from about 4 separate (and older) applications into a single, visually pleasing dashboard. 


The intent was to provide a centralized application where team users could track multiple tickets simultaneously without having to sign-in and remember the flows for all the individual apps.


![Untitled_Artwork.jpg](/images/content/jpl/jpl-0.jpg)


## WSPR - Waiver Signing


A lot of projects on JPL laboratory would go through very specific document flows that were internal. The waivers initially were paper-only. TBT.


To speed up the lab we built a a React / Django application that provided these documents and signing capabilities to JPL teams at large.

projects.content:
_Need to generally be ambiguous about the work. Hard to talk numbers_


# General Context


Sure Inc., focuses on building a platform that allows companies to own the entire insurance flow from choosing products to sell, generating documents, configuring pricing, triggering emails, etc. It’s a entirely configurable system.


## My Pod


The team I worked for built and maintained core features including documents, emails, webhooks, and pricing calculations (ROC). 🐬 


_maybe a graphic handling a lot of general structure_


A lot of engineers on my team really prided themselves on strong integration / unit testing and deep code reviews which really suited my engineering philosophies.


However, my team had to interface with several other teams including a group responsible for a solid component library.


## My Contributions


Unfortunately, due to restructuring I only worked on this team / division for about 6 months. But I made significant contributions to every domain except ROC. Additional work focused on refactoring existing code and adding QA automation tests.


## Documents


The UI underwent a fairly large refactor / improvement. Originally, the document hub was a rudimentary system with a simple UI. We added a lot of new functionality including

- Document contextual state management to handle save states across multiple components
- Document reordering built using React DnD’
- Document test mode that programmatically pulled variables and input options
- Improved error handling for a ton of backend validation edge cases
- Better trigger system that could handle file, section, or document generation conditions

## Emails / Webhooks


Simple work adding additional options for triggering emails and webhooks, but focused on refactoring a lot of hardcoded code for reusability.

projects.title: Porfolio
projects.description: Fully static site built entirely during GitHub workflows using React Router 7 framework. Leverages Notion for CMS project management and Claude for intelligent palette generation.
projects.content:
# It’s just a static website


At its core, yes, this is a static website. _Periodt_. 


But, underneath that, it has a lot more work put into it:

- Notion database as a makeshift CMS for managing project content
    - Automatic PR’s and CI on cron schedules when Notion databases are updated
- GitHub workflows to handle CI checks, GitHub Page Deployments, and Cron Jobs
    - E2E, Unit, and Linting to keep code clean and reusable and check for breaking changes in an age of Agentic coding
    - Sentry Error Logging and Monitoring
- Intelligent palette creation using Claude prompts in a workflow to generate swappable website color palettes based off project images

Frontend engineering is a lot more than just writing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript; though admittedly I love that part of the field, it’s a constantly evolving space.


## 💾 Notion Database


Leveraging Notion as a headless CMS requires a paid plan to access the Notion API. After receiving an API key, you can query individual databases and loop through rows and items.


![Portfolio Notion Database Setup](/images/content/porfolio/porfolio-0.jpeg)

- `Doc Name` - Corresponds to project title _(subject to change, honestly)_
- `Tags` - Added as project tags, just for extra knowledge / SEO perhaps, but might be useful for querying and sorting in the future
- `Favorites` - Boolean checkbox primarily used for generating specific palette themes
- `Description` - Project description on projects page
- `Color` - Theme color for the individual project page right up (like this one)

### Automatic PR and CI on Notion Changes


I [configured a cron job](https://github.com/deeplyfriedchicken/kevincunanan/blob/main/.github/workflows/fetch-notion.yml#L5) to run nightly which hits the Notion API and checks for changes. 


IF it detects changes, it’ll overwrite a JSON file and open a PR. GitHub is set for automatic merging as well, so this _should_ all run automatically without me needing to configure anything.


![image.png](/images/content/porfolio/porfolio-1.png)


## 🔬 GitHub workflows to handle CI/CD


Every push to main must be handled through a branch + PR. Pull requests can only get merged if CI checks pass. Once a PR is merged to main, we kick off a workflow to deploy to GitHub Pages.


![CI/CD workflow](/images/content/porfolio/porfolio-2.jpg)


## Testing & Linting

> quote on AI and importance of testing software

LLM’s and agents are quickly becoming an important part of the software engineering space. Anyone who’s not using the tools here is going to fall behind. However, the somewhat unsupervised nature of code means that testing has become more important. 


### Unit & E2E Tests


Basic strategies for unit and e2e happy path testing were implemented. The most important things to test are the Notion scripts and Project components and flows handling data.


### Linting


Linting checks run after completed agent task runs and on PR’s.


### Sentry


To monitor errors and failed jobs, I’ve added Sentry to the Notion data fetching scripts. My future feature is to add monitoring and dashboards for errors and general metrics.


We also added Sentry React to handle 404 errors, but hopefully I’ll catch and handle more errors in the future.


## 🎨 AI Generated Color Palettes


Attached to the `fetch-notion` workflow is a color palette generator. Introducing the `Favorites` property;  using AI, if there’s any projects with cover icons with that boolean property enabled, we feed Claude the logo and ask it to produce a color-accessible color palette.


![Fetch Notion + Claude Palette Workflow](/images/content/porfolio/porfolio-3.jpg)


I built a flexible theme picker using Tailwind and a `data-theme` property. These were static color palettes that were decided in Figma. However, I personally felt these lacked character and purpose in general. 


It’s a fun way to use AI and the Notion CMS together without creating a big risk for prompt injection on my site.
